steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper that presents M4, a dataset for black-box detection of machine-generated text spanning multiple generators, domains, and languages. Motivate the problem, contrast it with earlier detection work, list our contributions, and end with an outline of the paper.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- LLMs and the explosion of machine-generated content; misuse concerns
- Need for automatic detectors; limits of previous MGT detection work
- Our approach: multiple languages, LLMs, domains; SemEval-2024 Task 8
- Contributions
- Paper organization

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:

  - machine-generated content in news, social media, QA forums, educational and academic contexts
  - recent LLMs: ChatGPT, GPT-4, LLaMA 2, Jais -> remarkably fluent responses to varied queries
  - high quality -> attractive to replace human labor
  - concerns: misuse, e.g. spreading disinformation, disrupting education system
- Why automatic detection
  - humans only slightly better than chance at machine vs. human text
  - goal: help develop automatic detectors; build a diverse resource for training/testing MGT detectors
  - previous work: (i) one or two languages, typically English; (ii) single generator, e.g. ChatGPT; (iii) LLMs fine-tuned for specific tasks, e.g. MT or summarization; (iv) one domain, e.g. news
  - ours: multiple languages, various LLMs, diverse domains -> more general detection
  - dataset is basis of SemEval-2024 Task 8
- Contributions
  - M4: large-scale multi-generator, multi-domain, multi-lingual corpus; black-box scenario (only plain text, no access to generator or its outputs)
  - detector study: (a) across domains for one generator, (b) across generators for one domain, (c) domains x generators in multilingual setting, (d) data from different time periods; observations for future research
  - data and code released freely; repository to keep growing (new generators, domains, languages)
- Organization
  - Sec 2 related work
  - Sec 3 corpus collection: generators davinci-text-003, ChatGPT, GPT4, Cohere, Dolly2, BLOOMz; domains Wikipedia, WikiHow, Reddit, QA, news, paper abstracts, peer reviews; languages Arabic, Bulgarian, Chinese, English, Indonesian, Russian, Urdu
  - Sec 4 seven detectors
  - Sec 5 evaluation: across domains given generator (ChatGPT or davinci), across generators given domain (arXiv or Wikipedia), across languages
  - Sec 6 conclusion, future work

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Large language models (LLMs) are becoming mainstream and easy to access, and this has led to an explosion of machine-generated content in many channels, such as news, social media, question-answering forums, educational contexts, and even academic contexts. Recent LLMs such as ChatGPT, GPT-4, LLaMA 2, and Jais give remarkably fluent responses to a wide variety of user queries. Because the generated texts are of such high quality, it is attractive to use them to replace human labor in many scenarios. However, this raises concerns that they could be misused, for example to spread disinformation or to cause disruptions in the education system. steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Large language models (LLMs) are becoming mainstream and easy to access, and this has led to an explosion of machine-generated content in many channels, such as news, social media, question-answering forums, educational contexts, and even academic contexts. Recent LLMs such as ChatGPT, GPT-4, LLaMA 2, and Jais give remarkably fluent responses to a wide variety of user queries. Because the generated texts are of such high quality, it is attractive to use them to replace human labor in many scenarios. However, this raises concerns that they could be misused, for example to spread disinformation or to cause disruptions in the education system. Humans are only slightly better than chance at telling machine-generated texts from human-written ones, so we want to help the development of automatic detectors to mitigate the potential misuse of LLMs. In particular, we build a diverse resource that can be used for training and testing different models for detecting machine-generated text (MGT). Previous work on detecting MGT (i) focused on only one or two languages, usually only English, (ii) used a single generator, for example just ChatGPT, (iii) used LLMs fine-tuned for specific tasks, for example machine translation or text summarization, or (iv) considered only one domain, for example news. In contrast, we cover multiple languages, various LLMs, and several diverse domains, with the goal of enabling more general machine-generated text detection. Our dataset is the basis for SemEval-2024 Task 8. Our contributions are the following:

- We construct M4, a large-scale multi-generator, multi-domain, and multi-lingual corpus for detecting machine-generated texts in a black-box scenario, where there is no access to a potential generator or its outputs other than plain text.

- We study how automatic detectors perform from various perspectives: (a) different detectors across different domains for a specific LLM generator, (b) different detectors across different generators for a specific domain, (c) how domains and generators interact in a multilingual setting, and (d) how the detector performs on data generated in different time periods. From these experiments we draw a number of observations that can inform future research.

- We release our data and code freely, and we plan to keep growing our repository by adding new generators, domains, and languages over time.

The rest of the paper is organized like this. Section 2 discusses related work. Section 3 describes how we collected the corpus from multiple generators (including davinci-text-003, ChatGPT, GPT4, Cohere, Dolly2, and BLOOMz), multiple domains (including Wikipedia, WikiHow, Reddit, QA, news, paper abstracts, and peer reviews), and multiple languages (Arabic, Bulgarian, Chinese, English, Indonesian, Russian, and Urdu) for machine-generated text detection. Section 4 presents the seven detectors that we experiment with. Section 5 evaluates how they perform across domains given a generator (ChatGPT or davinci), across generators given a domain (arXiv or Wikipedia), and also across different languages. Section 6 concludes and points to possible directions for future work.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Large language models (LLMs) are becoming mainstream and easily accessible, ushering in an explosion of machine-generated content over various channels, such as news, social media, question-answering forums, educational, and even academic contexts. Recently introduced LLMs, such as ChatGPT, GPT-4, LLaMA 2 [1], and Jais [2], generate remarkably fluent responses to a wide variety of user queries. The high quality of the generated texts makes them attractive for replacing human labor in many scenarios. However, this raises concerns about their potential misuse, e.g., to spread disinformation or to cause disruptions in the education system [3]. Since humans perform only slightly better than chance when classifying machine-generated vs. human-written texts [4], we aim to facilitate the development of automatic detectors to mitigate the potential misuse of LLMs. In particular, we construct a diverse resource that could be used for training and testing various models for detecting machine-generated text (MGT). Previous efforts in detecting MGT (i) focused on only one or two languages, typically only English, (ii) used a single generator, e.g., just ChatGPT [5,6], (iii) leveraged LLMs fine-tuned for specific tasks, e.g., machine translation or text summarization [7], or (iv) considered only one specific domain, e.g., news [8,9]. In contrast, here we cover multiple languages, various LLMs, and several diverse domains, aiming to enable more general machine-generated text detection. Our dataset serves as the basis for SemEval-2024 Task 8 [10]. Our contributions are as follows:

- We construct M4: a large-scale multi-generator, multi-domain, and multi-lingual corpus for detecting machine-generated texts in a black-box scenario, where there is no access to a potential generator or its outputs except for plain text.

- We study the performance of automatic detectors from various perspectives: (a) different detectors across different domains for a specific LLM generator, (b) different detectors across different generators for a specific domain, (c) interactions of domains and generators in a multilingual setting, and (d) the performance of the detector on data generated in different time periods. From these experiments, we draw a number of observations that can inform future research.

- We release our data and code freely, and we plan to keep our repository growing, adding new generators, domains, and languages over time.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: Section 2 discusses related work. Section 3 describes the process of collecting the corpus from multiple generators (including davinci-text-003, ChatGPT, GPT4, Cohere, Dolly2, and BLOOMz), multiple domains (including Wikipedia, WikiHow, Reddit, QA, news, paper abstracts, and peer reviews), and multiple languages (Arabic, Bulgarian, Chinese, English, Indonesian, Russian, and Urdu) for machine-generated text detection. Section 4 presents the seven detectors we experiment with. Section 5 evaluates their performance across domains given a generator (ChatGPT or davinci), across generators given a domain (arXiv or Wikipedia), and across different languages. Finally, Section 6 concludes and points to possible directions for future work.
